[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of St. Vincent, is claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
DETERMINATION

[2] After considering the totality of the evidence, relevant documents, statutory provisions, counsel's submissions and case law, the panel finds the claimant failed to provide sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to discharge her onus establishing that a serious possibility of persecution based on a Convention ground exists or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in St. Vincent, if she were to return to St. Vincent.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[3] The panel finds, the claimant on a balance of probabilities, is a citizen of St. Vincent and has established her identity, absent any evidence to rebut the genuineness of the passport2 proffered to Canadian authorities in support of her identity.

[4] In assessing credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Orelien,3 stating that "one cannot be satisfied that the evidence is credible or trustworthy, unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so." [5] The panel was also guided by the Federal Court of Appeal in Dan-Ash,4 which stands for the proposition that an important indicator of credibility is the consistency with which a witness has told a particular story, including to Canadian immigration officials.

The panel draws a negative inference in this respect.

[9] The claimant alleged that she fled St. Vincent because of the threats and spousal abuse by XXXX. However, her testimony at the hearing indicates that she left St. Vincent, with four friends to attend a wedding in Canada on XXXX XXXX 2009. When the claimant was asked to name the friend whose wedding she came to attend, the claimant stated that she could not remember. When asked to explain the inconsistency between fleeing and traveling to attend a wedding she stated that she took the opportunity to seek help in Canada.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of St. Vincent, is claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
DETERMINATION

[2] After considering the totality of the evidence, relevant documents, statutory provisions, counsel's submissions and case law, the panel finds the claimant failed to provide sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to discharge her onus establishing that a serious possibility of persecution based on a Convention ground exists or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in St. Vincent, if she were to return to St. Vincent.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[3] The panel finds, the claimant on a balance of probabilities, is a citizen of St. Vincent and has established her identity, absent any evidence to rebut the genuineness of the passport2 proffered to Canadian authorities in support of her identity.
ALLEGATIONS AND CREDIBILITY ASSESSMENT

[4] In assessing credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Orelien,3 stating that "one cannot be satisfied that the evidence is credible or trustworthy, unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so." Serious internal inconsistencies, external inconsistencies, and implausibilities existed in the claimant's testimony.

[5] The panel was also guided by the Federal Court of Appeal in Dan-Ash,4 which stands for the proposition that an important indicator of credibility is the consistency with which a witness has told a particular story, including to Canadian immigration officials.

[6] The panel also took into consideration The Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution5 when approaching the process of the hearing and the facts in this case. All relevant factors, such as social and cultural context in which the claimant found herself, along with the issue of state protection and country conditions, were examined with consideration of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.

[7] The claimant's allegations are detailed in the Personal Information Form (PIF).6 In summary, the claimant alleges that she was in a common-law relationship with XXXX XXXX and was a victim of spousal abuse, beating and death threats. The claimant left him in 2006, and shortly after XXXX travelled to Canada. He married and lived there until 2009. After his return to St. Vincent he continued to threaten her.

[8] The claimant failed to mention XXXX in response to question 16 of the Claim for Refugee Protection in Canada form (CIC)7 instructing the claimant to list Spouse, common-law or same sex partner. When asked to explain the reason for omitting XXXX name the claimant explained that "she was not in a relationship with him". While the panel accepts her explanation as reasonable; however, the panel expects to have XXXX mentioned in response to question 43 instructing the claimant to state "Why are you asking for Canada's protection". The panel draws a negative inference in this respect.

[9] The claimant alleged that she fled St. Vincent because of the threats and spousal abuse by XXXX. However, her testimony at the hearing indicates that she left St. Vincent, with four friends to attend a wedding in Canada on XXXX XXXX 2009. When the claimant was asked to name the friend whose wedding she came to attend, the claimant stated that she could not remember. When asked to explain the inconsistency between fleeing and traveling to attend a wedding she stated that she took the opportunity to seek help in Canada.

[10] The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's inability to name the person whose wedding she attended, given her evidence that it cost her approximately $400 dollars to travel. To finance her trip she had to sell an "animal" and also get money from a friend. The panel also finds her explanation for the reason to travel to Canada not credible.

[11] Upon entry to Canada the claimant received authorization to stay until XXXX XXXX 2010.8 However, she did not claim asylum in Canada until 10 September 2012. The claimant testified that she did not try to extend her visitor visa. When asked to explain the reason for failing to regularise her stay or seek asylum in Canada she stated that in 2010, she spoke to the elder of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, L.B. She did not want to tell her friends her situation as they would think of her negatively and she was afraid. She further stated that she had spoken to a lawyer regarding getting a status in 2010, who required $5,000 dollars fee. The claimant was asked the reason she did not approach legal aid for assistance she stated that "I did not know." The claimant in support of her allegations submitted a letter from L.B.9 The lack of authentication of the letters leads the panel to question the letter's reliability and gives it little weight.

Furthermore, there is insufficient credible evidence before the panel to suggest that on a balance of probabilities XXXX would pursue the claimant in 2018, given that the claimant allegedly left him in 2006.

subthemes.text:
[12] The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation for the delay in claiming asylum in Canada for approximately two and half years as reasonable. The panel also notes the claimant's explanation in the PIF narrative stating that she was apprehensive and fearful to disclose her serious, personal and sensitive problems with strangers, "Including Canadian government-immigration officials, who I felt would casually disregard my plight as St. Vincent officials had done several times earlier and eventually force me to return to St. Vincent." 10 The panel is mindful of Gender Guidelines with respect to a woman's reluctance to disclose abuse to authorities, however, it is reasonable to expect the claimant who testified that she came to Canada to get help to approach the immigration officials after her authorization to stay expired, she had benefit of friends, church, and an employer to assist her.

[13] The panel finds it is reasonable to expect a person seeking international protection to ask for it at their earliest, in this case at least after her authorization of stay in Canada had expired and not approximately two and a half years later.

[14] The panel finds the claimant's actions not seeking asylum or regularizing her stay in Canada demonstrates lack of subjective fear of return to St. Vincent.

[15] In view of the cumulative effect of all of the above findings the panel finds the claimant's allegation about spousal abuse at the hands of XXXX on a balance of probabilities is not credible. This lack of credibility also extends to the statements submitted by her mother and daughter in support of the claimant's allegations; who basically recite the allegation the claimant has made in her narrative, and have interest in the outcome of the case. Furthermore, there is insufficient credible evidence before the panel to suggest that on a balance of probabilities XXXX would pursue the claimant in 2018, given that the claimant allegedly left him in 2006.

[16] The claimant has therefore not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture upon return to St. Vincent within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[17] The panel therefore concludes that XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee and not a person in need of protection.
DECISION
